### 13.5 Termination is a state, not an exception
- V1 This section specifies how a model ends its own run.
- V2 FlightCore's `SimulationTermination` idiom (model code throws, and the loop catches and logs it as informational) has no counterpart here (D-060). [D-060] (bold)
- V3 Graceful termination is model state, never an exception (D-060). [D-060] (bold)
- V4 It reaches the loop through declared machinery.
- V5 The discipline is that exceptions from model code are always abnormal (D-060). [D-060] (bold)
- V6 The wall-clock channel, through a front end's stop button (D-310), a device handle or code, is orthogonal and untouched. [D-310]
- V7 That is the operator path of the control plane (the separate atomic surface carrying pause, pace and stop).
- V8 The sim-time, model-detected channel specified here meets it at §12.4 and nowhere else. [§12.4]
- V9 The section covers, in order, detection and publication, placement and requesters, the policy per advance, the scan and the source order, unbounded runs, the termination record, ignored requests and post-terminal dynamics, and inspection beside the reads a run acts on.

#### Detection and publication
- V10 Detection is ordinary guard (the declared function that detects an event), handler and mode machinery (D-060). [D-060]
- V11 If the stop should be localized, declare the predicate (what a guard defines) as a sign-form event.
- V12 Such an event is localized (the crossing instant bracketed by root-finding over trial sweeps).
- V13 Touchdown overload is precisely a zero-crossing.
- V14 The boundary (a published consistency point) is localized to the crossing, and the handler sets `m.crashed`.
- V15 The snapshot (the immutable per-boundary publication) at the crossing instant carries the touchdown state.
- V16 Publication is a stop request (an output port of the framework enum `StopFlag`), declared where the stop's `Bool` is detected.
- V17 A port whose type is exactly `StopFlag` is a stop request, whoever publishes it (D-316). [D-316] (bold)
- V18 The enum is `@enum StopFlag NO_STOP STOP_REQUESTED`.
- V19 An enum is one leaf, pinned at every activation (§4.3), and cells (typed entries of the signal table) are stored per element type (§9.7), so every request in the model lands in one `StopFlag` block. [§4.3, §9.7]
- V20 The stop's `Bool` is gathered at its owning boundary in one visible block.
- V21 The landing gear `Ldg` from the example of §6.1 ORs its three legs through a junction (the ownership idiom, §6.2; the library, §13.7). [§6.1, §6.2, §13.7]
- V22 It wires the result into a `StopRequest` child, the library's spelling of a request, described below.
- V23 No level above it re-exports anything, because the loop reads the request where it is.
- V24 The library spelling is `StopRequest` (D-316). [D-316] (bold)
- V25 It is a stateless continuous leaf in the mould of `Constant` (§13.7). [§13.7]
- V26 Its one input is the stop's `Bool`, its one output the flag, and its reason is instance data.
- V27 [code block] # StopRequest — a stateless continuous leaf; its reason is instance data
- V28 Its output is consumed by nobody, which §6.1 allows silently (D-084). [§6.1, D-084]
- V29 `StopRequest` is continuous, so it refreshes at every boundary, `t` included (D-316). [D-316]
- V30 Assemblies are virtual for execution and rate scopes touch discrete children only, so one leaf sits anywhere in the tree (§10.5, D-019). [§10.5, D-019]
- V31 Fed by a discrete detector, it sees the tick at the tick's own boundary, because the boundary sweep walks the full execution order in topological order (§10.5, D-147). [§10.5, D-147]
- V32 The block holds no privilege.
- V33 Any component (a leaf or an assembly of components) may publish a `StopFlag` port directly.

#### Placement and requesters
- V34 Placement is checked at build.
- V35 Two placements are `IllegalPortType` (D-316). [D-316] (bold)
- V36 A `StopFlag` leaf nested inside a port of another type is refused with reason `:stop_flag_nested`, and a root input whose type carries a `StopFlag` anywhere with reason `:stop_flag_at_root`.
- V37 The first is refused because the build lists requests per port, so a request inside a struct field or a static array would have no listing of its own.
- V38 The second is refused because a request is the model's, never an operator's.
- V39 The operator's path is the control plane (§12.1). [§12.1]
- V40 A `StopFlag` input port places nothing and is left alone.
- V41 The requester roster (the build's list of stop requests, one `Requester(path, port, reason)` per `StopFlag` output port, in build order) names every request.
- V42 The build records one `Requester(path, port, reason)` per `StopFlag` output port, as the `requesters` of the activation's cell layout, index-aligned with the `StopFlag` block (D-316). [D-316] (bold)
- V43 The requester at index `i` owns the block's offset `i - 1`, and requester roster order is build order.
- V44 The reason is the publishing component's `stop_reason`, an optional declaration with default `""` (§8.2). [§8.2]
- V45 One reason serves all of a component's requests.
- V46 It is instance data on the component, never a port value.

#### The policy per advance
- V47 §12.6 declares the stop policy per advance, with `t_end` and `ignore_stop_requests` as keywords of `run!`, `replay!` and `step!`, and gives the value's lifetime. [§12.6]
- V48 Each of the three calls takes `Inf` and `()` as the defaults (D-255). [D-255]
- V49 The defaults belong to the calls that take the policy.
- V50 With no constructor defaults the trace header (the trace's fixed preamble, taken at boundary zero) has no policy to record (§11.5). [§11.5]
- V51 The termination record (the stopped-sim value naming how the run ended) carries the policy that actually ended the run.
- V52 Every request is honoured unless the advance ignores it (D-316). [D-316] (bold)
- V53 `ignore_stop_requests = :all` ignores every requester.
- V54 An iterable of strings names requesters by component path.
- V55 Each path is validated against the requester roster on every call, and duplicates collapse, in the order given.
- V56 A path naming no requester is `StopRequestInvalid`, collected over the given paths (Appendix C). [Appendix C]
- V57 A `t_end` that is not a non-negative real is `ArgumentInvalid`, refused before the ignore list is read.
- V58 Each advance builds a `StopPolicy` (the immutable value of `t_end` plus the ignored requester paths), and passes it to the loop with an ignore mask, one `Bool` per requester, as a second argument (D-316). [D-316]
- V59 A `t` hit reaches the loop as `frame!`'s return value (D-261, D-317), a `Bool` saying whether the frame was abandoned, never as a field of the policy or of the execution cursor (the field recording where execution stands). [D-261, D-317]
- V60 The loop then reads the requester off the snapshot it just published.

#### The scan and the source order
- V61 After every published boundary the loop scans the `StopFlag` block of the snapshot it just published, in requester roster order (D-316). [D-316] (bold)
- V62 Grid boundaries, `t` (§10.4) and boundary zero (the initialization boundary at `t₀`) all count (§14.5). [§10.4, §14.5]
- V63 The first honoured request reading `STOP_REQUESTED` initiates §12.4 shutdown with this snapshot as the final one. [§12.4]
- V64 The terminal snapshot is the terminal state.
- V65 There is no roll-back, and nothing §12.4 does not already do. [§12.4]
- V66 That terminal snapshot's status carries the run's final cumulative diagnostic counters (§11.8). [§11.8]
- V67 Every advance checks the latest snapshot for an honoured request before its first frame.
- V68 After `init!` that snapshot is boundary zero's, so an authored condition (the path-addressed sparse overlay that sets a build's state) already terminal ends the run at `t₀` with that snapshot final, integrating nothing.
- V69 A run that starts later ends where it started, advancing no frame.
- V70 The request is the author's and the ignore list the integrator's, and the ignore list sits beside `t_end` at the same declaration site.
- V71 The sources are consulted in a fixed order (D-203). [D-203] (bold)
- V72 The loop checks a pending control stop at frame top, then `t_end`, then the stop requests at each publication.
- V73 When two sources hold at one boundary, the recorded source is the first in that order (D-203). [D-203]
- V74 The rule authors are taught is this.
- V75 Stop requests are sampled at completed boundaries; declare a sign-form event if you need the stop localized.
- V76 Both shapes of the stop's `Bool` feeding a request work without framework latching.
- V77 A handler-set `m` flag is sticky by nature.
- V78 A transient stage-2 Bool is caught because the loop reacts to the first request it reads holding.
- V79 Compound stop logic composes in-model, as a monitor component reading the relevant signals and feeding one request.
- V80 That is the same move §12.5 made for scripts. [§12.5]

#### Unbounded runs
- V81 An unbounded run is allowed (D-255). [D-255] (bold)
- V82 `run!(sim)` with `t_end = Inf` and no honoured request is the interactive session's ordinary shape, and the operator interrupt (Ctrl-C, read as a control-plane stop) is its escape (§12.4). [§12.4]
- V83 The model may have no requester, or the advance may ignore them all.
- V84 `run!` raises `UnboundedRun` before the loop starts, into the loop's own diagnostic cell (the per-writer cell for runtime diagnostics), and the status record carries it (§11.8, D-255, D-316). [§11.8, D-255, D-316]
- V85 Its message says which of the two cases holds.
- V86 The advisory fires in `:live` only.
- V87 A `run!` in `:replay` is bounded by the recording, whatever its policy says (§12.7, D-218). [§12.7, D-218]
- V88 [code block] sim = Simulation(world; h = 1//50)          # no policy here: the deployment has none

#### The termination record
- V89 The termination record names the source, as a typed value (D-203). [D-203] (bold)
- V90 The run's termination record carries its outcome, and the `StopPolicy` of the advance that ended it (D-255). [D-255]
- V91 The record holds four things, the final boundary time, the terminating policy, the source and the tail residue (the post-account diagnostics the run's-end sweep folds in).
- V92 §11.8 specifies that sweep. [§11.8]
- V93 The time is always present, because boundary zero precedes every record and a throw inside boundary zero writes none (§12.6, D-233). [§12.6, D-233] (bold)
- V94 The source follows the diagnostic convention, so its type is its identity and its payload is plain data (§13.2, D-203). [§13.2, D-203]
- V95 There are four source types.
- V96 `EndTimeReached` means `t_end`'s frame completed.
- V97 It has no payload.
- V98 The record's own `t` is the fact, and the bound that was configured is in the record's own policy.
- V99 `ModelRequestedStop` means an honoured stop request read `STOP_REQUESTED`.
- V100 The payload is the requester's component path, its port and its reason.
- V101 When two requests hold at one boundary, the record names the first in requester roster order (D-316). [D-316]
- V102 `ControlRequestedStop` means a control-plane stop.
- V103 The payload is its issuer, the requesting device, `:code` or `:interrupt` (§12.1). [§12.1]
- V104 `LoopError` means the abnormal entry of §13.6. [§13.6]
- V105 The payload is the propagated cause.
- V106 A throw inside the frame reaches the record with the `Model` already marked `:inconsistent` by its own catch, and the simulation reads `errored`.
- V107 A loop fault outside the frame, in the pacer, a yield or the tail, closes the run as `stopped` with the `Model` consistent at its last settled boundary, since only the `Model`'s own catch sites mark it (D-317). [D-317]
- V108 The record covers both exactly alike.
- V109 A `stopped` simulation therefore answers "why did it stop?" without its consumer reconstructing the answer from the clock.
- V110 It answers "how did the stop go?" from the same value.
- V111 The operator interrupt is a tag on an ordinary stop, not a source type of its own, because nothing failed (D-203). [D-203] (bold)
- V112 Appendix C gains nothing from it. [Appendix C]

#### Ignored requests and post-terminal dynamics
- V113 An ignored request is still a cell in every snapshot, so the log records when validity broke even on a run that continued (D-316). [D-316]
- V114 Two uses share the mechanism, validity breakdown and scenario completion.
- V115 The reason string is what tells a reader which, and the framework never will.
- V116 Post-terminal dynamics are the model's job, and that is a feature.
- V117 `robot2d` is FlightApps' self-balancing robot in Flight.jl, which throws `LostBalance`, a `SimulationTermination`, past 45° of tilt.
- V118 It throws when it falls, because it has no other way to say "my dynamics are no longer meaningful".
- V119 Here it declares the fall as an event, switches to a frozen mode, and feeds `fallen` to a stop request.
- V120 The frozen mode is a mode-dependent `x_deriv`, machinery the model already has.
- V121 Honoured, the request ends the sim at the fall.
- V122 Ignored, the sim integrates a frozen robot, which is well-defined, unlike an uncaught throw.
- V123 The discipline forces models to have well-defined terminal states, which is better modeling (D-060). [D-060]

#### Inspection and the reads a run acts on
- V124 The rejected mechanisms, litigated in D-060 and D-316, are predicate closures such as `stop_when = snap -> …`, root-type-declared stop policy, which the per-advance policy is not, `terminal` event flags, a control-plane capability for components, observation-by-path (an advance naming a deep path into any public output), and the `Bool` face re-exported level by level to the root and named by the advance, which fell to stop requests. [D-060, D-316]
- V125 D-060 also rejected blessed (explicitly sanctioned by the spec) terminal types scanned from the tree, an arm the stop request supersedes on its own terms. [D-060]
- V126 The observation-by-path line leaves doctrine behind it, narrowed by D-316. [D-316]
- V127 Inspection is human-facing, has no effect on run semantics, and legitimately sees every public cell.
- V128 The log retaining the full table, a front end's panels rendering a component's ports, and inspection under replay (the ordinary loop re-driven from a recorded trace) are all inspection.
- V129 A read the run acts on changes what the run does, and it reads only what the model declared for it, never an arbitrary cell.
- V130 The stop scan is the one such read.
- V131 It reads the `StopFlag` block, which holds nothing but the requests their authors declared by type.
- V132 §13.3 draws the same line for path resolution, client by client. [§13.3]
- V133 The ignore list addresses the `Build`'s requester roster, a build product like the root-input list.
- V134 It binds at an advance, a stopped-sim point where conditions already address state by path (§14.1). [§14.1]
- V135 The requester is loud at inspection, since the requester roster and the termination record name it.
- V136 Substitution is answered by the ignore list, and disabling is one keyword.
- V137 The trigger is the author's knowledge and the ignore list the integrator's.
- V138 Output devices are the other half of the same doctrine.
- V139 Their reads are inspection bindings on snapshot paths (§11.2). [§11.2]

### 13.6 Abnormal shutdown: one tail, two entries
- V140 A failure on the loop's side can arrive in the middle of a boundary (a published consistency point).
- V141 The run must still end through the shutdown tail of §12.4, which starts from a final snapshot (the immutable per-boundary publication). [§12.4]
- V142 This section gives the abnormal path, the reason it is safe, the two entries charted, the record it writes, tail hygiene, and what an errored simulation keeps and refuses.
- V143 The abnormal path discards the failed boundary, promotes the previous snapshot to final, and rejoins the ordinary tail (D-030). [D-030] (bold)
- V144 The protocol becomes one tail with two entry points.
- V145 Graceful entry follows a completed final boundary, and abnormal entry follows a discarded one.
- V146 Everything downstream of "final snapshot" runs identically.
- V147 That covers sticky stopped, waiters woken through the boundary-counter plus `Condition` path, the hooks `unblock!` and `shutdown!`, and named joins with timeout.
- V148 Those waiters observe stopped rather than a new boundary, so no task of a device (an attached participant in the periphery) hangs.
- V149 The abnormal path rests on this.
- V150 The boundary is all-or-nothing outside the loop (D-030). [D-030]
- V151 That is why a `StepError` cannot break §12.4. [§12.4]
- V152 Sweeps (passes through the execution order) write into table blocks.
- V153 Integration intermediates live in framework-owned integrator buffers.
- V154 They never live in the scratch of a component (a leaf or an assembly of components).
- V155 That scratch is its workspace (declared by allocation and excluded from state semantics), as §7.3 defines it. [§7.3]
- V156 The only externally visible act is snapshot publication at the very end of the sequence.
- V157 A boundary that throws has published nothing.
- V158 The last published snapshot is a complete, consistent boundary by construction, and it is still the newest thing any device, logger or waiter has seen.
- V159 [code block] graceful entry                      abnormal entry
- V160 This fills the seat §12.4 reserved for it. [§12.4]
- V161 A loop-side failure runs the same protocol from the catch path (D-030). [D-030]
- V162 The termination record (the stopped-sim value naming how the run ended) covers this entry too.
- V163 Its source is `LoopError`, and the payload is the propagated cause (§13.5, D-203). [§13.5, D-203]
- V164 Tail hygiene follows from the hooks being user code too.
- V165 Each is individually caught and logged.
- V166 Shutdown therefore runs to completion even if a device's hook misbehaves.
- V167 The join timeout already bounds a hook that hangs rather than throws.
- V168 What is lost is quarantined.
- V169 A throw inside the frame leaves the stores (the framework-owned homes of a component's `x`, `s` and `m`) possibly holding mid-boundary values, such as a half-written `m` or integration intermediates.
- V170 They are retained on the errored simulation for post-mortem inspection.
- V171 An errored simulation is terminal, not resumable, and the reproduction tool is trace replay (re-driving the ordinary loop from the session's recorded inputs), not resurrection (§12.6, D-059, D-387). [§12.6, D-059, D-387]
- V172 The stopped-sim services enforce that non-resumability by refusing an errored simulation outright (`ServiceLifecycle`, §14). [§14]
- V173 The roster operations refuse it with them (§11.3, D-232). [§11.3, D-232]
- V174 Inspection is reading, but `attach!` configures a run that cannot follow.
- V175 The published record (snapshot chain, log, trace) ends at the last consistent boundary.
- V176 Nothing downstream of the sim ever sees half a boundary.
